questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to apply simple bit-tricks succinctly and reason about edge cases without loops. It also shows understanding of bitwise adjacency relationships across 64 bits.

## Key Concepts

- Bitwise AND and right shift
- Detecting pattern overlap without branching
- Constant-time evaluation on fixed width integers

## Code Example

```javascript
function hasConsecutiveOnes(n) {
  // n treated as a 64-bit value; bitwise ops apply to 32-bit in JS
  return (n & (n >>> 1)) !== 0;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you extend to count how many adjacent pairs exist?
- How would you test correctness with edge inputs like all zeros, all ones, alternating patterns?

Tests the ability to decompose a 128-bit integer into 32-bit lanes and recombine them in a different order without using branches.

- Representing a 128-bit integer as two 64-bit halves (hi and lo)
- Extracting 32-bit lanes using bit masks and shifts

## Why This Is Asked
Shows mastery of low-level bit tricks and edge-case handling in constrained environments.

## Key Concepts
- Next permutation with fixed popcount using bit hacks
- Branchless arithmetic for speed
- Fixed-width overflow behavior

## Code Example
```javascript
uint64_t nextHigherWithSamePopcount(uint64_t n) {
  uint64_t c = n & -n;
  uint64_t r = n + c;
  return (((n ^ r) >> 2) / c) | r;
}
```

- How would you adapt for arbitrary width (128-bit)?
- How does this interact with compiler optimizations and undefined behavior in signed contexts?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests the ability to apply a well-known bit-twiddling technique (compact1by1) to shrink bit width without branches—a common optimization in performance-critical code.

## Key Concepts

- **Cascade of masks and shifts**: Each iteration merges pairs of bits, then pairs of pairs, doubling the packed width at each step.
- **Fixed constants**: Each mask (0x5, 0x3, 0xF, etc.) in binary is 0101, 0011, 1111—selecting the lower half of each bit group.
- **Branch-free**: Contains no conditionals; executes in constant time.

## How It Works

The algorithm packs even-positioned bits (0, 2, 4, ..., 62) from the 64-bit input into a 32-bit output. At each stage, we first propagate each bit to its neighbor (x | x >> k), then mask to keep only the desired positions. This doubling process continues until all even bits are consolidated into the lower 32 bits. The final cast extracts the result as a 32-bit integer.

## Key Concepts
